question: Broker Ana sponsors sales agent Luis, who represents a buyer. Luis also happens to be the buyer's cousin. During negotiations, Luis learns the buyer would pay up to $15,000 more than the current offer, but does not disclose this to the seller. Later, the seller's agent asks Luis directly whether the buyer would pay more, and Luis truthfully declines to answer while remaining professional. Luis's conduct here is:
choice_a: A violation, since Luis must always disclose a client's maximum price if asked directly
choice_b: A violation solely because Luis is related to the buyer
choice_c: Improper because Luis represents the buyer at all, given the family relationship
choice_d: Proper, since Luis owes a duty of confidentiality to his buyer-client regarding the buyer's negotiating position and is not required to volunteer or confirm it
explanation: As the buyer's representative (not an intermediary), Luis owes the buyer a fiduciary duty of confidentiality regarding the buyer's negotiating limits and is not obligated to disclose that information to the other side, even when directly asked -- he must simply avoid affirmatively misrepresenting the buyer's position. The family relationship alone does not create a violation, though best practice calls for disclosure of the relationship to all parties.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies -- narrative cases); TRELA agency/confidentiality principles

question: Broker Sam receives two competing written offers on a listed home on the same afternoon. The seller had earlier told Sam, verbally only, 'Don't bother showing me anything under $300,000.' One offer is $295,000, the other is $310,000. Sam's proper course of action is to:
choice_a: Present both offers to the seller anyway, since the seller's instruction to withhold offers was not documented in writing as TREC standards of conduct require
choice_b: Withhold the $295,000 offer entirely based on the verbal instruction alone
choice_c: Present only the higher offer and never mention the lower one existed
choice_d: Decide independently which offer better serves the seller's interests without seller input
explanation: A broker's duty to present all offers can only be limited by the seller's specific written instruction; a verbal-only comment does not satisfy that standard, so Sam must still present both offers and let the seller make the final decision, while also now securing that preference in writing going forward.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies); National/General Broker Content Outline V.B.1 (seller representation) -- Duties to Client

question: Sponsoring broker Devon discovers that sales agent Priya has been collecting property management rent checks and depositing them into her own personal checking account 'temporarily' before forwarding the net amount to owners each month. Devon's required response under 22 TAC Section 535.2 and Section 535.146 is to:
choice_a: Allow the practice to continue since owners were always eventually paid in full
choice_b: Immediately stop the practice, ensure all funds are properly accounted for and moved to the firm's designated trust account, and address the serious compliance failure through corrective action
choice_c: Take no action unless a specific owner files a complaint
choice_d: Simply ask Priya to be more careful going forward with no further investigation
explanation: Priya's practice is a clear violation of the rule that a sales agent may never maintain a trust account -- rent and other trust money must go through the broker's designated trust account -- and Devon's own supervisory duty under 22 TAC Section 535.2 requires immediate corrective action, not merely a passive acknowledgment, given the serious commingling/misappropriation risk this practice creates regardless of past outcomes.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: Broker Maria is acting as an intermediary in a transaction, with sales agents Ben and Carla appointed to represent the buyer and seller, respectively. Ben asks Maria to tell Carla that his buyer-client 'really needs' the seller to cover $5,000 in closing costs, without saying whether the buyer would still proceed if the seller refuses. Maria's proper role here is to:
choice_a: Refuse to convey any negotiating message under any circumstances as intermediary
choice_b: Add her own personal recommendation that the seller should agree, since she wants the deal to close
choice_c: Convey Ben's message as instructed while remaining neutral, without independently editorializing or adding her own opinion favoring either side
choice_d: Tell Carla the buyer will definitely walk away if the seller refuses, even though Ben never said that
explanation: As the neutral intermediary, Maria's role is to facilitate communication between the appointed associated license holders without becoming an advocate for either side or embellishing/fabricating information beyond what was actually authorized to be communicated -- she must convey Ben's actual message accurately, not editorialize or overstate it.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sections 1101.559-1101.561 (Intermediary Practice); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A buyer's home inspection reveals evidence of a prior foundation repair not disclosed on the seller's disclosure notice. The seller's agent, upon learning this from the buyer's agent, discovers the seller genuinely did not know about the repair (performed by a prior owner and never disclosed to the current seller). The seller's agent's best course of action is to:
choice_a: Ignore the new information entirely since the original disclosure notice has already been delivered
choice_b: Instruct the seller to deny knowledge indefinitely, since the seller did not personally know at signing
choice_c: Tell the buyer's agent it is not the seller's agent's problem to address
choice_d: Advise the seller to amend the disclosure notice with the newly discovered information and discuss next steps with the buyer's side, since disclosure obligations continue even after initial delivery once new material information becomes known
explanation: A seller's (and by extension, the seller's agent's) disclosure obligation is ongoing -- newly discovered material information should prompt an amended disclosure, since knowingly withholding a material fact once discovered, even if the seller was innocent of the original omission, can create liability once the seller becomes aware and fails to update the disclosure.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008 (Seller Disclosure Requirements); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's sponsored sales agent, working a listing under the office's standard exclusive right-to-sell agreement, personally purchases the listed property at a below-market price without disclosing to the seller that the buyer is the agent themselves, using a shell LLC to mask the purchase. This conduct is:
choice_a: A serious breach of fiduciary duty and grounds for significant discipline, since an agent must disclose any personal interest in a transaction involving a client
choice_b: Permitted, as long as the LLC's name does not include the agent's own name
choice_c: Acceptable since real estate agents are permitted to buy any property they personally list
choice_d: A matter of no concern to TREC, since only civil courts would have jurisdiction
explanation: An agent's undisclosed self-dealing -- purchasing a client's listed property while concealing their own identity and interest -- is a severe breach of the fiduciary duties of loyalty and disclosure and a clear ground for TREC discipline, regardless of the entity structure used to obscure the purchase.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652 (Grounds for Suspension or Revocation); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker managing a residential rental property for an out-of-state owner collects a $2,000 security deposit from a new tenant. The broker's trust account already holds deposits for four other properties managed for different owners. TREC's expectation under 22 TAC Section 535.146 is that the broker will:
choice_a: Keep entirely separate physical bank accounts for every individual property managed
choice_b: Maintain records sufficient to reconcile and account for each owner's/tenant's funds separately within the pooled trust account, even though all deposits may be held in a single designated account
choice_c: Combine all deposits into the broker's own operating account for simplicity
choice_d: Refuse to accept new deposits until existing tenant deposits are refunded
explanation: TREC permits a broker to maintain a single designated trust account holding funds for multiple clients/properties, but the broker must keep records sufficient to reconcile and individually account for each owner's and tenant's funds within that pooled account -- separate bank accounts per property are not required, but sloppy or absent individual accounting is a violation.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: During a listing presentation, a broker tells a seller that the broker 'guarantees' the home will sell within 60 days at the listed price, based purely on the broker's optimism rather than any market data. The home does not sell within 60 days, and the seller later complains to TREC. The broker's statement most likely constitutes:
choice_a: Harmless puffery with no regulatory significance
choice_b: A binding contractual warranty enforceable exactly as written with no consequence to the broker's license
choice_c: A misleading representation, since a guarantee of a specific sale outcome is not a matter of opinion but an assurance a broker cannot actually make or control
choice_d: A statement with no bearing on TREC standards, since it was made only during a listing presentation, not a signed contract
explanation: Unlike subjective opinion statements ('this is a beautiful home'), a specific guarantee about an outcome the broker cannot actually control -- like a guaranteed sale timeline -- crosses from permissible puffery into a misleading representation that can expose the broker to TREC discipline, particularly if a seller relied on that guarantee in making listing decisions.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies); National/General Broker Content Outline V.D.5 (fraud and misrepresentation)

question: A sponsored sales agent, working outside the scope of activities the broker authorized in writing, independently agrees to reduce the brokerage's commission by half to 'help close the deal' without consulting the broker. The broker later objects. Under 22 TAC Section 535.2, this scenario illustrates the importance of:
choice_a: Nothing; a sales agent always has unlimited authority to set commission terms unilaterally
choice_b: The broker's total inability to ever correct or address an agent's unauthorized commitment
choice_c: A situation with no supervisory dimension at all, since it involves only pricing, not legal compliance
choice_d: Clearly documenting the scope of an agent's authorized activities in writing, since undocumented or exceeded authority creates both compliance and financial exposure
explanation: This scenario underscores why 22 TAC Section 535.2 requires brokers to document the scope of sponsored agents' authorized activities in writing -- clear documentation gives the broker a stronger basis to address unauthorized commitments (like unilaterally altering compensation terms) after the fact, whereas undocumented authority leaves ambiguity about what the agent was actually permitted to agree to.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's sponsored sales agent uses a TREC-promulgated residential contract but, at the buyer's request, hand-writes in an unusual clause purporting to waive the buyer's statutory right to terminate during the option period retroactively after the option period has already ended, in exchange for a $500 payment from the seller. This modification is concerning primarily because:
choice_a: It involves the agent effectively drafting custom legal terms altering statutory/contractual rights after the fact, which risks unauthorized practice of law and potential unenforceability
choice_b: Hand-written additions to TREC-promulgated forms are always automatically void
choice_c: The $500 amount is below the legal minimum for any addendum
choice_d: Only the buyer, not the agent, faces any risk from this arrangement
explanation: An agent drafting custom, retroactive contractual language altering a party's rights goes well beyond filling in blanks on an approved form and risks unauthorized practice of law; such a provision should be referred to an attorney to draft properly, both to protect the parties' actual legal interests and to protect the agent from disciplinary exposure.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline III.C (Unauthorized Practice of Law) and VII (Case Studies), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker's trust account reconciliation reveals that the account balance is $3,200 higher than the sum of all individual client ledgers. Investigation reveals the broker's own commission from a recent closing was accidentally left in the trust account instead of being transferred to the operating account. The broker's correct response is to:
choice_a: Leave the extra funds in the trust account indefinitely, since having more money than required causes no harm
choice_b: Promptly transfer the broker's own earned commission out of the trust account into the operating account, correcting the discrepancy and documenting the correction
choice_c: Use the extra funds to cover a different client's shortfall elsewhere in the account
choice_d: Ignore the discrepancy since it favors the broker rather than harming a client
explanation: Even a trust account surplus (rather than a shortage) reflects a commingling problem -- the broker's own earned funds should not sit in the trust account any longer than necessary -- and the correct, documented fix is to promptly move those funds to the appropriate operating account, maintaining a clean and accurate trust account that matches client ledgers exactly.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money -- commingling prohibition); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker is asked by a longtime client to represent both the buyer and the seller in a private, off-market sale between two parties who already know and trust each other, with no other broker involved. To lawfully proceed representing both, the broker must:
choice_a: Simply proceed informally, since both parties already trust each other and consent seems implied
choice_b: Decline the assignment entirely, since representing both parties is never permitted in Texas under any circumstance
choice_c: Obtain written consent from both parties to intermediary representation, consistent with TRELA Section 1101.559, before proceeding
choice_d: Represent only the party who first contacted the broker, automatically
explanation: Even where the parties have an existing personal relationship and trust each other, Texas law still requires the broker to obtain the parties' written consent to intermediary status under Section 1101.559 before lawfully representing both sides of the same transaction -- informal or assumed consent does not satisfy the statutory requirement.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559 (Broker Acting as Intermediary); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A brokerage's designated broker learns that a sponsored sales agent has consistently failed to provide required written representation disclosures at first contact across multiple recent transactions, a pattern the broker only discovered through a routine file audit. The broker's appropriate response includes:
choice_a: No action, since none of the affected clients personally complained
choice_b: Immediate, automatic reporting of the broker's own license to TREC for revocation with no opportunity to correct the practice
choice_c: Simply firing the agent with no further documentation or corrective process
choice_d: Corrective action with the agent, additional training, and closer supervisory review going forward, documented in the broker's own compliance records
explanation: A pattern of repeated representation-disclosure failures under Section 1101.558, discovered through the broker's own supervisory review, calls for documented corrective action and enhanced oversight -- both to fix the underlying compliance gap and to demonstrate the broker's good-faith exercise of the supervisory duty required under 22 TAC Section 535.2, which matters considerably if TREC later investigates.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558; Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A buyer's agent appointed under an intermediary arrangement privately advises the buyer to offer $10,000 below asking price based on the agent's market analysis. The listing-side appointed agent, working for the same intermediary broker, separately advises the seller to hold firm at full price. This dynamic is:
choice_a: Consistent with how appointed intermediary representation is designed to work, since each appointed agent may advocate and advise their assigned party individually while the broker itself stays neutral
choice_b: A violation of intermediary rules, since appointed agents may never give differing advice to each side
choice_c: Only permissible if the two appointed agents first agree with each other on a joint recommendation
choice_d: Prohibited because only the broker, not the appointed agents, may communicate with the parties
explanation: This is exactly how properly structured intermediary representation with appointed associated license holders is designed to function under Section 1101.560 -- each appointed agent may individually advise and advocate for their assigned party's negotiating position, while the broker itself remains the neutral intermediary facilitating the transaction overall.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.560 (Associated License Holder Acting as Intermediary); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's review of a closed transaction file reveals that earnest money was deposited by the sales agent nine calendar days after receipt, with no written agreement from the principals authorizing a delayed timeline. This delay most directly violates:
choice_a: No rule, since nine days is within a commonly assumed 30-day grace period
choice_b: 22 TAC Section 535.146's requirement to deposit trust money within two business days absent a different written agreement of the principals
choice_c: Only an internal office guideline with no regulatory significance
choice_d: A rule that applies only to brokers, never to sponsored sales agents handling funds on the broker's behalf
explanation: Absent a written agreement extending the timeline, trust money must be deposited by the close of business on the second working day after receipt under 22 TAC Section 535.146; a nine-day delay with no documented extension is a clear violation, and because sales agents act on the broker's behalf in handling trust money, the deadline applies functionally to however the funds move through the office.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's sponsored sales agent tells a prospective buyer that a neighborhood is 'a great choice for families like yours' after the buyer mentions having young children, intending it as friendly rapport-building rather than steering. Reviewing this conduct, the broker should recognize that:
choice_a: This comment raises no fair housing concern since no harm was intended
choice_b: Fair housing protections do not cover familial status in Texas
choice_c: Even well-intentioned comments referencing familial status when recommending or discouraging particular neighborhoods risk violating fair housing steering prohibitions and should be avoided in office training
choice_d: Only comments about race, not familial status, ever implicate steering concerns
explanation: Fair housing steering violations do not require malicious intent -- even a well-meaning comment that references a protected class (like familial status) in recommending where a buyer with children should or shouldn't live can constitute unlawful steering, which is precisely why broker-level fair housing training must address these subtler, good-faith-but-still-improper scenarios.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C (Fair Housing); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's sponsored sales agent representing a seller receives an offer contingent on the buyer selling their current home first. The seller wants to keep marketing the property to other buyers while this contract is pending, hoping to find a better, non-contingent offer. The appropriate TREC-promulgated tool for this situation is:
choice_a: Simply terminating the contingent contract immediately upon receiving any new offer, with no formal addendum
choice_b: Refusing to accept any contingent offer under Texas law
choice_c: Ignoring the seller's request, since sellers may never continue marketing under a pending contract
choice_d: A kick-out clause/addendum allowing the seller to continue marketing and accept a backup or replacement offer under specified conditions while the contingent contract remains pending
explanation: TREC-promulgated addenda address exactly this scenario -- allowing a seller to continue marketing a property under a contingent contract and providing the contingent buyer a specified window to remove the contingency or lose the contract if a better offer materializes, giving the seller flexibility while still respecting the contingent buyer's contractual rights during that window.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline V.A (Promulgated Contracts, Forms, and Addenda) and VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's property management client asks the broker to stop making agreed repairs to a rental unit and instead simply raise the rent to cover ongoing maintenance issues, without addressing habitability concerns the tenant has properly reported. The broker's ethical and legal obligation, given Property Code Chapter 92 landlord duties, is to:
choice_a: Advise the owner-client of the landlord's statutory repair obligations and the legal risk of ignoring properly reported habitability issues, even though the broker acts as the owner's agent
choice_b: Simply follow the owner's instructions without comment, regardless of statutory landlord duties
choice_c: Immediately terminate the property management agreement with no discussion
choice_d: Ignore the issue since tenant habitability concerns are solely the tenant's problem
explanation: While a property manager acts as the owner's agent, that agency relationship does not excuse the broker from advising the client about applicable legal obligations -- here, the landlord's statutory duty to repair conditions materially affecting health and safety under Property Code Chapter 92 -- since failing to do so could expose both the owner and, potentially, the managing broker to liability.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 92.001 et seq. (Landlord-Tenant); National/General Broker Content Outline V.B.3 (property management agreement)

question: A broker discovers that a sponsored sales agent has been using a personal cell phone and unofficial email account to negotiate transactions, with no copies of those communications saved to the brokerage's official file system. From a supervision standpoint, this practice is concerning primarily because it:
choice_a: Is entirely appropriate, since agents have full discretion over how they communicate with clients
choice_b: Undermines the broker's ability to conduct the periodic transaction review required under 22 TAC Section 535.2 and creates recordkeeping gaps
choice_c: Only matters if a client specifically complains about the communication method
choice_d: Has no bearing on the broker's supervisory obligations, since supervision applies only to written contracts, not communications
explanation: A broker's supervisory review obligation under 22 TAC Section 535.2 depends on having visibility into how transactions are actually being handled; an agent conducting substantive negotiations through untracked personal channels creates a real recordkeeping and compliance gap that a well-run brokerage's office policy should specifically address.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- periodic review of transaction documents); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)
